In [[statistical mechanics]], the '''hard hexagon model''' is a 2-dimensional [[Lattice model (physics)|lattice model]] of a gas, where particles are allowed to be on the vertices of a [[hexagonal lattice|triangular lattice]] but no two particles may be adjacent.

The model was solved by {{harvs|authorlink=Rodney J. Baxter|last=Baxter|first=Rodney|year=1980|txt}}, who found that it was related to the [[Rogers–Ramanujan identities]].

==The partition function of the hard hexagon model==

The hard hexagon model occurs within the framework of the [[grand canonical ensemble]], where the total number of particles (the "hexagons") is allowed to vary naturally, and is fixed by a [[chemical potential]]. In the hard hexagon model, all valid states have zero energy, and so the only important thermodynamic control variable is the ratio of chemical potential to temperature ''μ''/(''kT''). The exponential of this ratio, ''z'' = exp(''μ''/(''kT'')) is called the '''activity''' and larger values correspond roughly to denser configurations.

For a triangular lattice with ''N'' sites, the [[grand partition function]] is

:<math>\displaystyle \mathcal Z(z) = \sum_n z^n g(n,N) = 1+Nz+ \tfrac{1}{2}N(N-7)z^2+\cdots</math>

where ''g''(''n'', ''N'') is the  number of ways of placing ''n'' particles on distinct lattice sites such that no 2 are adjacent. The function &kappa; is defined by

:<math>\kappa(z) = \lim_{N\rightarrow\infty} \mathcal Z(z)^{1/N} = 1+z-3z^2+\cdots</math>

so that log(&kappa;) is the free energy per unit site. Solving the hard hexagon model means (roughly) finding an exact expression for &kappa; as a function of ''z''.

The '''mean density''' &rho; is given for small ''z'' by

:<math>\rho= z\frac{d\log(\kappa)}{dz}  =z-7z^2+58z^3-519z^4+4856z^5+\cdots.</math>

The vertices of the lattice fall into 3 classes numbered 1, 2, and 3, given by the 3 different ways to fill space with hard hexagons. There are 3 local densities &rho;<sub>1</sub>, &rho;<sub>2</sub>, &rho;<sub>3</sub>, corresponding to the 3 classes of sites. When the activity is large the system approximates one of these 3 packings, so the local densities differ, but when the activity is below a critical point the three local densities are the same.  The critical point  separating the low-activity homogeneous phase from the high-activity ordered phase is <math>z_c = (11+5\sqrt5)/2 = \phi^5 = 11.09017....</math> with [[golden ratio]] ''φ''. Above the critical point the local densities  differ and in the phase where most hexagons are on sites of type 1 can be expanded as

:<math> \rho_1 = 1-z^{-1}-5z^{-2}-34z^{-3}-267z^{-4}-2037z^{-5}-\cdots</math> 
:<math> \rho_2=\rho_3 = z^{-2} + 9z^{-3} + 80z^{-4} +  965z^{-5}-\cdots.</math>

==Solution==
The solution is given for small values of ''z''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''z''<sub>''c''</sub> by

:<math>\displaystyle z=\frac{-xH(x)^5}{G(x)^5}</math>

:<math>
\kappa = \frac{H(x)^3 Q(x^5)^2} {G(x)^2}
\prod_{n\ge 1} \frac{(1-x^{6n-4})(1-x^{6n-3})^2(1-x^{6n-2})} 
{(1-x^{6n-5})(1-x^{6n-1})(1-x^{6n})^2}
</math>

:<math>\rho =\rho_1=\rho_2=\rho_3= \frac{-xG(x)H(x^6)P(x^3)}{P(x)}</math>

where
:<math>G(x) = \prod_{n\ge 1}\frac{1}{(1-x^{5n-4})(1-x^{5n-1})}</math>

:<math>H(x) = \prod_{n\ge 1}\frac{1}{(1-x^{5n-3})(1-x^{5n-2})}</math>

:<math>P(x) = \prod_{n\ge 1}(1-x^{2n-1}) = Q(x)/Q(x^2)</math>

:<math>Q(x) = \prod_{n\ge 1}(1-x^n).</math>

For large ''z''&nbsp;>&nbsp;''z''<sub>''c''</sub> the solution (in the phase where most occupied sites have type 1) is given by 
:<math>\displaystyle z=\frac{G(x)^5}{xH(x)^5}</math>

:<math>
\kappa = x^{-\frac{1}{3}}\frac{G(x)^3 Q(x^5)^2} {H(x)^2}
\prod_{n\ge 1} \frac{(1-x^{3n-2})(1-x^{3n-1})} 
{(1-x^{3n})^2}
</math>

:<math>\rho_1 = \frac{H(x)Q(x)(G(x)Q(x)+x^2H(x^9)Q(x^9))}{Q(x^3)^2}</math>

:<math>\rho_2=\rho_3 = \frac{x^2H(x)Q(x)H(x^9)Q(x^9)}{Q(x^3)^2}</math>

:<math>R=\rho_1-\rho_2= \frac{Q(x)Q(x^5)}{Q(x^3)^2}.</math>

The functions ''G'' and ''H'' turn up in the [[Rogers–Ramanujan identities]], and the function ''Q'' is the [[Euler function]], which is closely related to the [[Dedekind eta function]]. If ''x'' = e<sup>2&pi;i&tau;</sup>, then ''x''<sup>&minus;1/60</sup>''G''(''x''), ''x''<sup>11/60</sup>''H''(''x''), ''x''<sup>&minus;1/24</sup>''P''(''x''), ''z'', &kappa;, &rho;, &rho;<sub>1</sub>,  &rho;<sub>2</sub>, and &rho;<sub>3</sub> are [[modular function]]s of &tau;, while ''x''<sup>1/24</sup>''Q''(''x'') is a modular form of weight 1/2. Since any two modular functions are related by an algebraic relation, this implies that the functions ''&kappa;'', ''z'', ''R'', ''&rho;'' are all algebraic functions of each other (of quite high degree) {{harv|Joyce|1988}}. In particular, the value of ''&kappa;''(1), which [[Eric Weisstein]] dubbed the '''hard hexagon entropy constant''' {{harv|Weisstein}}, is an [[algebraic number]] of degree 24 equal to 1.395485972...&nbsp;({{oeis|A085851}}).

==Related models==
The hard hexagon model can be defined similarly on the square and honeycomb lattices. No exact solution is known for either of these models, but the critical point ''z''<sub>c</sub> is near {{val|3.7962|0.0001}} for the square lattice and {{val|7.92|0.08}} for the honeycomb lattice; ''&kappa;''(1) is approximately 1.503048082...&nbsp;({{oeis|A085850}}) for the square lattice and 1.546440708... for the honeycomb lattice {{harv|Baxter|1999}}.
